sections.heading: The derivative as a limit at a point

questions.q: Use $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ to find $f'(3)$ for $f(x)=x^2-2x$.
Use the alternate form $f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$ to find $f'(2)$ for $f(x)=x^3$.
Explain why $f(x)=|x-2|$ is not differentiable at $x=2$, computing the one-sided derivatives.
questions.answer: Left-hand: $\lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{|h|}{h}=-1$. Right-hand: $\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{|h|}{h}=1$. Since these disagree, $f'(2)$ does not exist (the graph has a corner).

questions.q: State three conditions under which a function fails to be differentiable at a point, with a brief description of each (e.g. corner, cusp, vertical tangent, discontinuity).
questions.answer: (1) A corner — one-sided derivatives disagree, as with $|x|$. (2) A vertical tangent line — the slope becomes infinite, as with $\sqrt[3]{x}$ at $x=0$. (3) A discontinuity — if $f$ isn't continuous at a point, it can't be differentiable there, since differentiability implies continuity.

sections.heading: Visualizing the derivative as a tangent slope

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=3x^2-x$ (from an earlier problem) with its tangent line at $x=1$, where $f'(x)=6x-1$.
parts: Confirm the tangent line's slope matches $f'(1)$.
Explain what it means graphically for the line to be "tangent" at this point.
answers: $f'(1)=6(1)-1=5$, matching the tangent line $y=5x-3$, which has slope $5$.

Being tangent means the line touches the curve at $x=1$ and has the same instantaneous rate of change (slope) as the curve at that exact point, so locally the line is the best straight-line approximation to the curve there.

questions.q: A ball's height is $h(t)=-5t^2+30t+1$ (meters, seconds). Use the limit definition of the derivative (or the power rule, since it agrees) to find $h'(t)$, then find the ball's velocity at $t=2$.
questions.answer: $h'(t)=-10t+30$. At $t=2$: $h'(2)=-20+30=10$ m/s (the ball is still rising).

sections.heading: Comparing average and instantaneous rate of change

questions.q: For $f(x)=x^2$, find the average rate of change on $[1,3]$, then compare it to the instantaneous rate of change $f'(2)$ at the midpoint $x=2$.
questions.answer: Average rate: $\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1}=\frac{9-1}{2}=4$. Instantaneous rate: $f'(x)=2x$, so $f'(2)=4$. They match exactly here, because for a quadratic, the average rate over an interval always equals the instantaneous rate at the interval's midpoint.
